relationships.description: The page or screen reads from or invokes an application module or service class, for example by injecting it or calling its methods to load or change state.
relationships.evidence: The view's source file imports or injects the component, such as a store, service or provider, and calls its methods from lifecycle hooks or event handlers.

relationships.description: The screen reads or writes records in a persistent table, document collection or bucket directly, without going through an API layer.
relationships.evidence: The view's code or loader runs a database client query, such as a Firestore, Supabase or IndexedDB call, against that named collection or table.

relationships.description: The screen calls a specific HTTP method-and-path endpoint to fetch or submit the data it displays or edits.
relationships.evidence: The view's loader, hook or event handler issues a fetch or generated-client call to that method and URL path.

relationships.description: The screen reads its displayed data from a derived database view or materialized view instead of from base tables.
relationships.evidence: The view's data loader queries the named database view, for example with a SELECT against it or a client call that names it.

relationships.description: The screen contains buttons, links or menu entries that users activate, and these controls are defined independently and could be reused on other screens.
relationships.evidence: The view's template or JSX places the action control, such as a button or link component with an onClick or href, inside its markup.

relationships.description: The screen includes a region that is a placement of a reusable library sub-view, which also exists outside this particular screen.
relationships.evidence: The view's markup includes a shared sub-view component imported from a library or shared directory, with the sub-view's ref set.

relationships.description: The screen arranges its children according to a declared layout specification covering grid, flex, spacing and width rules.
relationships.evidence: The view's root container carries the layout configuration, for example grid or flex CSS classes or a layout object referenced in the view spec.

relationships.description: The screen obtains the data it displays through a declared binding that names the source, such as an API, a store or a static value, and the field path selected from it.
relationships.evidence: The view spec or code declares a data binding, for example a useQuery or store selector, or a dataConfig entry attached to the view.

relationships.description: The screen owns an inline, non-routable region that exists only as part of this screen and has no meaning without it.
relationships.evidence: The view spec defines the sub-view inline with no ref, or the view file declares a local section component used only by that view.

relationships.description: The screen can only run on a particular runtime or platform product, such as a browser engine, a Node SSR runtime or a native OS version.
relationships.evidence: package.json engines, the browserslist setting or the platform manifest declares the runtime that the view's rendering requires.

relationships.description: The screen presents and edits one business concept, such as an Order detail page or a Customer record screen.
relationships.evidence: The view's route, title and bound data model all correspond to the named business entity, for example the route /orders/:id loads an Order.

relationships.description: The screen is the UI surface whose usage is intended to produce a specific, measurable result, such as a checkout page tied to a target conversion rate.
relationships.evidence: Product or analytics documentation links the screen's tracked events or funnel to the outcome's target metric.

relationships.description: The screen is the concrete user-facing access point through which users reach an application component's services.
relationships.evidence: Architecture documentation or the route table identifies the view as the GUI entry point of the component's user interface.

relationships.description: The screen is the surface on which users carry out the steps of a business process, such as a claim submission screen for claims intake.
relationships.evidence: Process documentation or a user story maps the process steps to the view, and the view's actions perform those steps.

relationships.description: The screen is the concrete delivery of a user-perceivable product feature.
relationships.evidence: The feature's ticket or spec names the view's route or screen, and the view is gated by that feature's flag.

relationships.description: The screen is built as a concrete means of advancing a qualitative stakeholder goal, such as improving self-service.
relationships.evidence: A design brief or traceability matrix links the view to the goal it was created to advance.

relationships.description: The screen points to the structured record schema that defines the shape of the data it displays or submits.
relationships.evidence: The view's code imports the type, interface or JSON schema for the entity, or validates its form against it.

relationships.description: The screen is named as, or corresponds to, a protected UI area that authorization decisions are made about.
relationships.evidence: The access-control model lists the view's route or screen identifier as a resource with permitted operations.

relationships.description: The screen places and draws a specific configured occurrence of a library component as part of its display.
relationships.evidence: The view's template or JSX contains the library component element with its prop values at that position.

relationships.description: The screen depends on an error-display configuration that determines how load or action failures are shown to the user.
relationships.evidence: The view declares an error boundary, errorElement or errorConfig entry that specifies the notification severity and message text.

relationships.description: Users must hold a specific permission before the screen will open or display its content.
relationships.evidence: A route guard, middleware or the view code checks the permission string, such as can('orders:read'), before rendering.

relationships.description: The screen is accessible only to users assigned a particular role, such as Admin.
relationships.evidence: The route definition or guard on the view declares the required role, for example roles: ['admin'] or hasRole('admin').

relationships.description: The screen cannot function without an infrastructure capability such as CDN hosting, an identity provider or a push-notification service.
relationships.evidence: The view's code or deployment configuration calls the infrastructure service's SDK or endpoint, for example an auth provider or a storage SDK.

relationships.description: The screen fulfills a specific verifiable requirement, so that its behavior meets that requirement's acceptance criteria.
relationships.evidence: The requirement's acceptance tests exercise the view, or a traceability matrix maps the requirement ID to the view.

relationships.description: The screen's access behavior conforms to the rules of a named access-control policy.
relationships.evidence: Security review records or the policy's target definitions show the view's route evaluated under that policy, with matching guard behavior.

relationships.description: The screen makes an application service usable by presenting a user interface for that service's operations.
relationships.evidence: The view's actions invoke the service's operations, and the service documentation lists the view as its user-facing channel.

relationships.description: The screen is a working surface provided for people acting in a business role, such as an approver's review queue.
relationships.evidence: UX personas, the route's role guard or the navigation menu configuration designate the view for that role.

relationships.description: The screen is a channel through which customers or staff receive a business service, such as an online claims portal page.
relationships.evidence: Service design documentation lists the view as a touchpoint of the business service.

relationships.description: The screen exists to address the concerns and needs of a particular stakeholder group.
relationships.evidence: Design research, personas or requirements trace the view to that stakeholder's concerns.

relationships.description: The screen subscribes to, or emits, an application event in order to react to state changes, for example refreshing when an OrderPlaced event occurs.
relationships.evidence: The view's code registers an event listener or subscription for, or dispatches, the named event.

relationships.description: The screen relies on a layout configuration to position its children.
relationships.evidence: The view references the layout configuration in its spec or root container classes.

relationships.description: The screen authenticates its API calls using a declared credential mechanism, such as a bearer token or an OAuth flow.
relationships.evidence: The view's API client attaches credentials in the form the scheme specifies, for example an Authorization: Bearer header, and the called operations reference that scheme.

notes: uses.layoutconfig duplicates applies.layoutconfig; keep applies. aggregates.subview and composes.subview overlap and need a ref-set versus inline distinction. renders.componentinstance overlaps with aggregates.actioncomponent. realizes.motivation.goal should be supports-goals. maps-to is a data-mapping predicate and is misused for outcome and businessobject. serves.applicationservice is inverted: services serve the UI.
